opus-5.5.text:
I think the core mechanism is actually pretty simple, and it's one that economists have understood for a long time, even if they haven't usually applied it to AI. The basic idea is that if you can automate labor, you change the fundamental dynamics of economic growth.

Right now, the economy has inputs like capital and labor. We can accumulate capital: we invest, build more factories, more computers, more machines. But labor is essentially fixed by population, and population grows slowly. That means as you pile up capital, you run into diminishing returns, because each additional machine has fewer workers to operate it or complement it. That's a big part of why growth in frontier economies has been stuck around two percent a year.

What AI does, if it gets good enough to substitute for human workers across most tasks, is turn labor into something you can accumulate the way you accumulate capital. You can build more compute and run more copies of AI systems, so effective labor becomes a reproducible input. Once both capital and labor can be scaled up through investment, you get something much closer to increasing or at least constant returns to the things you can accumulate. That feedback loop, where output gets reinvested into more compute, which produces more AI workers, which produces more output, is what drives the very rapid growth in the model.

In GATE specifically, we model this as a gradual process. There's a spectrum of tasks in the economy, and each requires some amount of effective compute to automate. As investment flows into hardware and software, and as algorithmic progress makes compute more efficient, more of those tasks cross the automation threshold. Each step makes AI more economically valuable, which justifies more investment, which automates further tasks. So it's not a single moment where everything switches over. It's a process that accelerates as it goes.

There's also a second channel, which is that AI can accelerate R&D itself, including research on AI. That can speed things up further. But I'd emphasize that even without a dramatic intelligence explosion through software, the plain economics of making labor accumulable already gets you growth rates far above anything we've historically seen, potentially twenty or thirty percent a year or more once automation is broad enough.

The key point people often miss is that you don't need exotic assumptions to get this result. You just need AI that can do most of what human workers do, and standard growth economics does the rest. The bottlenecks that matter, like how fast we can build fabs, energy infrastructure, and data centers, and how much compute it actually takes to automate the hardest tasks, determine the timing. But the direction is pretty robust.

r001.rationale: The response describes task automation through investment and algorithmic progress and says AI-accelerated R&D can speed growth; it does not state that GATE excludes general-economy productivity growth as an endogenous result of research or investment.

r002.rationale: It identifies making labor accumulable through AI workers as the core mechanism driving GATE’s rapid projected growth.

r003.rationale: It explains that output can be reinvested in compute to produce more AI workers, making labor expandable through investment like capital.

r004.rationale: It calls labor automation the central mechanism and R&D an additional channel, but does not state that output is more elastic to labor-force scaling than to R&D.

r005.rationale: It says accumulating capital with labor essentially fixed leads to diminishing returns, explaining why scaling production eventually runs into growth limits.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the core mechanism in GATE is actually fairly simple once you strip away the details of the model. The main thing driving the economic impact is that AI becomes a substitute for human labor across an increasing fraction of tasks, and the inputs to AI, compute and the capital that produces compute, are things you can accumulate in a way you fundamentally can't accumulate human workers.

Right now, the economy has this bottleneck where labor is a fixed factor. You can build more machines, more factories, more software, but the number of people who can operate them and make decisions and do the cognitive work grows at maybe one percent a year. That's why returns to capital eventually diminish. You get more capital per worker, and each additional unit does less.

What AI does in the model is it breaks that. If you can convert compute into something that functions as labor, then labor stops being fixed. You can reinvest output into more chips, more datacenters, more energy, and that directly expands your effective workforce. So you get a feedback loop: more output lets you build more compute, more compute gives you more effective labor, and that produces more output. Capital stops hitting diminishing returns because the thing it was running up against has been removed.

The second piece is automation itself. In GATE we model the economy as a bunch of tasks, and AI can automate a growing share of them as training compute scales up. The important subtlety is that automating, say, half of tasks doesn't give you anywhere near half the economic benefit. The remaining human-performed tasks become the bottleneck, and they soak up most of the value. The really massive impact only shows up when you get close to full automation, because that's when the last bottlenecks disappear and the reinvestment loop can run unconstrained.

So when people see the headline numbers, growth rates of twenty or thirty percent a year or more, that's not coming from AI making existing workers a bit more productive. It's coming from the economy transitioning from one where labor is scarce and slow-growing to one where the effective labor supply is just another manufactured good you can scale. That's a regime change, not an incremental improvement, and that's really the heart of the mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI automation as scaling with training compute, but does not state that GATE excludes general-economy productivity growth as an endogenous result of research or investment.

r002.rationale: It identifies AI as a way to expand effective labor and calls the shift to a scalable effective labor supply the heart of the mechanism.

r003.rationale: It explains that output can be reinvested in compute infrastructure, which expands the effective workforce and creates a feedback loop.

r004.rationale: It contrasts scalable AI labor with slowly growing human labor and mentions diminishing returns to capital, but does not state that output is more elastic to labor-force scaling than to R&D.

r005.rationale: It explains that adding capital per worker eventually yields diminishing returns when labor remains fixed, conveying limits to growth from scaling production under fixed constraints.

astra-6.text:
I think the main mechanism is that AI can make the production of intelligence much more scalable. Today, if you want more research or engineering work done, you generally need more people with the relevant skills, and training those people takes a long time. With AI, you can potentially expand that capacity by investing in compute and running more copies of capable systems.

That creates a feedback loop. Better AI helps you do more research, including research that improves AI itself. It can also help develop better chips and improve the technologies used throughout the economy. Those improvements make it possible to produce more output and invest more resources in further progress.

So the big effect isn't just that AI saves time on a fixed set of tasks. It's that it can change the rate at which we develop new technologies and expand productive capacity. How large that effect becomes depends on the bottlenecks that remain—physical infrastructure, experiments, and tasks that AI can't yet perform. But that feedback between automation, investment, and technological progress is the central mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response does not state what GATE excludes; it instead describes research and investment as part of a feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It mentions running more copies of AI systems, but does not clearly identify AI workers expanding the effective labor force as GATE’s main mechanism.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that output can be reinvested to expand the labor force or compare that expansion to capital.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison between output’s responsiveness to labor-force scaling and to R&D.

r005.rationale: It mentions infrastructure and other bottlenecks, but does not explain that scaling production under fixed technology eventually limits growth.

sol-6.1.text:
The main mechanism is that AI could make cognitive labor reproducible. If you want more human researchers or engineers, you have to train people, which takes a long time. With AI, once you have a sufficiently capable system, you can run more copies by investing in computing infrastructure.

That creates a feedback loop: more capable AI helps you do research and develop better technology, including better AI. And as the economy grows, you can invest more in the infrastructure needed to run those systems, which gives you more research capacity again.

So the big effect isn’t just that everyone gets a productivity boost from having an assistant. It’s that investment can expand the supply of cognitive work, and that work can accelerate technological progress. How large the effect becomes depends on how quickly that process runs into bottlenecks elsewhere in the economy.

r001.rationale: The response describes research-driven feedback, but does not state that GATE excludes general-economy productivity growth as an endogenous result of research or investment.

r002.rationale: It identifies reproducible cognitive labor and the ability to run more AI copies as the central mechanism expanding the supply of cognitive work.

r003.rationale: It says economic growth can fund more computing infrastructure, but does not explain reinvesting output to expand the labor force by analogy with expanding capital.

r004.rationale: It does not compare the output response to labor-force scaling with the response to R&D.

r005.rationale: It mentions possible bottlenecks elsewhere in the economy, but does not state that scaling production with fixed technology eventually limits growth.
